description:
Eastern Kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus)

18 May 2016
Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge
Oklahoma State Highway 49
Indiahoma, Comanche County, Oklahoma

A single Eastern Kingbird was observed perched on a wire fence off to the side of Oklahoma State Highway 49 at the Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge. A migratory bird, the Eastern Kingbird spends its year between North and South America. It winters in South America across a broad swath of the continent in a northwestern to central direction. According to All About Birds, while in South America Eastern Kingbird mostly feeds on fruit. It flies north to reproduce and spend its spring and summer and crosses the Caribbean and Central America while hugging the Gulf Coast of Mexico wending its way into Texas and the rest of the United States and Canada. Once there, it claims nearly the entire eastern two-thirds and most of the northwest of the United States and its Canadian territory extends from the Pacific Coast to the Atlantic. A truly transcontinental bird, Eastern Kingbird is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. The Wichita Mountains Wildlife Refuge is administered by the US Fish and Wildlife Service of the US Department of the Interior.

Source: "Eastern Kingbird," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, range map, photographs, description, resources, accessed 5.21.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Eastern_Kingbird/id

description:
Eastern Kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus)

5 July 2016
Ray Roberts Lake State Park, Isle Du Bois
Pilot Point, Denton County, Texas

A still standing tall Eastern Cottonwood snag served in the late afternoon and early evening as a welcoming roost for several species of birds as they came and went through the area before nightfall. It was plainly evident that the main resident was the voluble male Red-winged Blackbird (not pictured here) who made clear to all that this was his territory and his snag, but other birds could visit so long as they put up with his singing, or his repeated if melodic declaration of place and belonging. The single female Red-winged Blackbird, clearly this one's partner, said nothing but watched vigilantly from another snag nearby. Amid this larger scene appeared this Eastern Kingbird who looked like it might be a first-year bird as we think we detected a bit of yellow at the gape. It was difficult to tell since the game of shadow and light that occurs right before and during dusk had begun when we took these pics. But the Eastern Kingbird stayed for about 10 minutes at its chosen perch before continuing on its way. Eastern Kingbird is a transcontinental traveler in the Western Hemisphere since it spends its spring and summer in Canada and the United States where it brings forth the next generation. By early fall Eastern Kingbird reverses this migratory route. In doing so it migrates through South Texas past Mexico and Central America and on into the South American continent. Once there, Eastern Kingbird claims half the continent from the northern reaches to the central regions as far south as the northeastern corner of Argentina. It makes effective use of South America's spring and summer much as it does when it travels north to reproduce. This is a quest for eternal spring perhaps but it has everything to do with optimizing ideal conditions for its survival as a species. Because of its extensive presence throughout both continents of the Western Hemisphere, Eastern Kingbird is one of its quintessential authentic residents. Ray Roberts Lake State Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

Source: "Eastern Kingbird," All About Birds, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Cornell University, range map, description, photographs, resources, accessed 6.7.16, https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Eastern_Kingbird/id

description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
I love fledgling season. I've never seen an Eastern Kingbird nest but I got to see some cute fledglings. Sharing my experience.
Photo 1:  I had just arrived at the lake and as soon as I stepped out of my car I heard a ruckus high in a tree top.  Had to use my camera to see what it was.  I could not get very close so these shot are heavily cropped.  Two eastern kingbird fledglings were yelling loudly for someone to come and feed them.  I've never seen an eastern kingbird nest and these were my first fledglings.  Did not spot a nest anywhere near.  One seems to be yelling at its sibling.  
Photo 2:  While I was watching, a parent flew over and perched and for a few seconds the babies and parent just stared at each other.  
Photo 3:  The silence only lasted a few seconds then the babies started begging for food loudly and the parent started yelling too for some reason.  The parent did not have any food for them.
Photo 4:  As the babies continued to beg, the parent flew a little closer on the tip of the tree on a seed ball.  I felt so sorry for the hungry babies with their open mouths pointed up at the parent.  It was obvious the parent had no food for them.  
Photo 5:  A minivan pulled up in the parking lot and some people with 3 loudly barking dogs got out.  The parent bird immediately flew to perch right by the babies and I got this last shot before all 3 flew off and out of sight.  Hopefully the babies got fed soon.  I loved getting to see this cute family.

Mom Brought Me A Dragonfly!

Where's My Dragonfly?

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; the final day of a three-day trip to Walker, Louisiana and back, taking a very circuitous route through the Panhandle to iNat several counties that we had rarely or never visited before. I have now photographed at least one bird species in each of Florida's 67 counties!

As we approached State Road 59 while driving on US-98, at 1530, I had intended to continue driving east so that we would arrive home at a reasonable hour (by 2000). But Val wanted to visit the refuge, saying that she gets to visit maybe once every two years, and since it's 6 miles away and the time was "still early," then we needed to visit. We drove straight to the lighthouse, stopping briefly only at East River Pool/Stony Bayou 1. A strong frontal system moved through east to west at 1650, lasting maybe 25 minutes, and dumping much rain. We were at the lighthouse when the storm hit, so we waited out the worst of it, then drove back north. When we again reached East River Pool/Stony Bayou 1, we were inundated with Eastern Kingbirds heading east or perched in the marsh, in shrubs, and in the few oaks. From 1730 to 1820, we tried to count the size of the flock, which continued moving through for more than 40 minutes and extended for at least one-half mile -- a huge kingbird swarm was visible over the pinewoods to the north. Our estimate of 2,500 Eastern Kingbirds was very likely an underestimate, perhaps by one or more orders of magnitude. Many swallows, including 22 Purple Martins, were also moving east following the storm front. After we left this site and continued north, we saw no other kingbirds, indicating that the flight was limited in width. We left the refuge at 1834 and continued east on US-98. We stopped at Perry for dinner, and arrived back at Bayonet Point at 0002 Monday morning.

description:
I found this eastern kingbird in the Little Missouri National Grassland a couple of nights ago (5-21-2024), perched in the grass as it waved back and forth in a stiff breeze.  Though it's spring in North Dakota, the somewhat cool nights and days the past week or so have kept the worst of the flying bugs at bay but there are still sufficient numbers to keep the birds busy.  These are among the flycatchers and they often hunt from a perch, flying up to capture a bug, then returning to their perch.  They're also travelers, for they are migratory birds and though they're fairly common in North America, they winter in Central and South America.  

You'll probably see a LOT of "documentary"-style bird images as I experiment with these more often.  Shooting birds-in-flight is akin to shooting skeet the size of pennies, I do believe (and I haven't shot skeet since probably the 90's  lol), with a few unprintable mutters, to boot!  lol
